correctness.rationale: Ferrari's symbol and optimized J=3 coefficients reproduce δ_3. Its derivative is (2−sqrt(2))(z−2−sqrt(2)/2) times the strictly positive quadratic z²−(1+sqrt(2))z+1+sqrt(2). This gives a unique real minimum and fixes the positive-real-pole regime. For P_q(Rx)/(1−x), expand the normalized cubic factors (1−tx)(1−2ux+νx²) to get F/c_0²=(1−ν)(1−2tu+t²ν), with ν=R²/|z_+|² and the second factor positive. The coefficients of the expanded symbol give F=−vR²G(R); the five positive Bernstein coefficients of G' and endpoint signs in the supplied interval isolate the only crossing. At the coalescence of the real roots the identity still holds with t=1, and G(R_c)>0 ensures that the positive double root is not dominant. Below q_* the simple positive pole gives a strictly positive leading coefficient. Above q_* there is no positive pole on the convergence circle; applying Pringsheim to either sign of an allegedly one-sided tail proves infinitely many coefficients of each strict sign. At q_* the competing complex poles must be controlled: direct residue comparison reduces A>2|B| to (R+Re z_+)|T−z_+|²>2R(T−R)². The quoted Vieta/rational boxes give a lower bound 15.627192309 against an upper bound 9.41696994, so equality in the modulus comparison still yields eventual strict positivity. Formal coefficient recurrence independently supports the stated lag-four sign defect at q=1. These are eventual sign statements, not all-lag or full-solver stability statements.
residual_risks: High-precision bisection gives q_*≈0.6108597918577594647; the frozen decimal differs by about 1.1e−15. The exact definition and rigorous bracket, and hence the theorem, are unaffected.
